Write a matrix in matrix styling, not in the plain italic of a scalar.
This holds for the predictor matrix $\mX$ in every file you edit:
notes, assignments, solutions, slides and note sheets.
A plain italic $X$ reads as a random variable or a single number.
In a group that uses shared macros (see [Using shared macros](#using-shared-macros)),
write the predictor matrix with the matrix macro `\mX`.

Keep two objects apart, because they are not the same matrix:

- The *predictor matrix* holds the raw inputs.
  Its rows are the predictor vectors $\vx_i$ of the $n$ observations.
  Write it `\mX`.
- The *design matrix* holds the inputs after any feature map and the intercept trick.
  Its rows are the design vectors $\vfeatmap(\vx_i)$.
  Write it `\design(\mX)`, or `\design` for short.

The same split holds for one observation:
the predictor vector is `\vx`, and the design vector is `\vfeatmap(\vx)`.
Without a feature map or an intercept column,
the design matrix equals the predictor matrix, but say so rather than reuse one symbol for both.

::: {#exm-predictor-vs-design-matrix}

## Predictor matrix and design matrix

> ❌ Let $X$ be the design matrix, and fit $\hat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y$.
>
> ✅ Let $\mX$ be the predictor matrix and $\design(\mX)$ the design matrix.
> The fitted coefficients solve the normal equations for $\design(\mX)$.

The ✅ version shows which matrix holds the raw inputs
and which holds the columns the model uses.

:::
